title: Number of Islands
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated full-grid merging scans versus DFS/BFS "sinking" each island once.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an m by n grid of "1" (land) and "0" (water), return the number of islands, where an island is a group of land cells connected 4-directionally (horizontally or vertically, not diagonally).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","grid of \"1\"s and \"0\"s"],["Output","Number of connected land regions (islands)"],["Goal","For every unvisited land cell, run DFS/BFS to sink its entire connected landmass, counting how many such searches start"],["Constraints","Up to 300 by 300 grid"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Count connected regions of a value on a grid\"","The classic grid connected-components counting problem, solved via DFS or BFS \"sinking\" each discovered island"]]}

blocks.text: This is a grid version of connected-components counting: every time an unvisited land cell is found, it must belong to a NEW island (since anything connected to a previously found island would already be marked visited). A DFS or BFS from that cell, spreading to all 4-directionally adjacent land cells and marking them visited ("sinking" them), correctly discovers and consumes the entire island in one search.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting Separate Landmasses on a Satellite Map
blocks.text: Picture counting distinct landmasses on a satellite map made of a grid of land and water pixels. Starting from any unmarked land pixel, spreading outward through every directly touching land pixel and marking them all as "counted" reveals the full extent of one landmass before moving to look for the next one.

blocks.caption: Each unvisited land cell starts a new island; DFS/BFS sinks the entire connected landmass

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Scanning the grid cell by cell, any land cell not yet visited must belong to an island not yet counted.

Observation 2: Running DFS (or BFS) from that cell, recursively visiting every 4-directionally adjacent land cell and marking each visited (for instance, by changing it to water, or using a separate visited array), correctly discovers the ENTIRE connected island in one search.

Observation 3: Incrementing a counter each time such a fresh search is STARTED (not for every cell visited) correctly counts the total number of distinct islands.
This leads to scanning every cell, running DFS/BFS from each still-unvisited land cell, and counting how many such searches are started.

Conceptually, repeatedly scan the entire grid, merging any two land cells into the same group whenever a new direct connection between different groups is discovered, looping until a full scan produces no further merges.
Why the code is written this way

items: Repeatedly merging groups until no changes occur eventually reaches the correct grouping.
This costs many redundant full-grid scans; a single DFS/BFS per unvisited land cell directly discovers each entire island in one pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((rows times cols) squared) worst case, due to repeated full scans.
Space: O(rows times cols) for the group map.
Limitation: a single DFS/BFS from every still-unvisited land cell discovers each entire island in one pass, without repeated scanning.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Scan the grid cell by cell. Whenever a "1" (land) cell is found, increment the island count, then run DFS (or BFS) from that cell, recursively "sinking" it and every connected land cell (setting them to "0", or marking them visited in a separate structure) so they are never counted again. Continue scanning until every cell has been processed.
Scan the grid once, running DFS/BFS from each still-unvisited land cell, counting how many searches are started.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Cell","Action"],"rows":[["(0,0)=\"1\"","new island, DFS sinks (0,0),(0,1),(1,1), count=1"],["(2,2)=\"1\"","new island, DFS sinks just (2,2), count=2"]]}

blocks.text: DFS (or BFS) from any land cell correctly visits and "sinks" every land cell reachable from it via 4-directional connections (its entire island), so starting a fresh search only when a land cell is STILL marked "1" (unvisited) guarantees each distinct island is discovered exactly once, and the running count of such fresh searches exactly equals the number of islands.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows times cols).
Space: O(rows times cols) recursion depth worst case.

blocks.text: Number of Islands is the quintessential grid-based connected-components counting problem, a direct application of the flood-fill technique.

items: Using 8-directional (including diagonal) connectivity when the problem specifies only 4-directional.
Forgetting to mark cells visited (sink them) during the DFS/BFS, causing infinite recursion or incorrect recounting.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["An entirely water grid","Returns 0, no islands."],["An entirely land grid","Returns 1, one single connected island."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "this is connected-components counting via DFS/BFS, applied to a grid instead of an adjacency list" connects this problem immediately to a familiar technique.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "count connected regions on a grid", think: DFS/BFS from each unvisited cell, counting how many searches are started.

items: How would you also find the AREA of the largest island (Max Area of Island), not just the count?
Flood Fill and Max Area of Island, both closely related grid DFS/BFS problems.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The repeated-merging brute force costs O((rows times cols) squared) worst case; the DFS/BFS-per-unvisited-cell approach costs O(rows times cols), the standard efficient solution.

items: Pattern: grid connected-components counting via DFS/BFS flood fill.
Core Idea: every unvisited land cell starts a new island; DFS/BFS sinks its entire connected landmass.
Time: O((rows times cols)^2) worst case for the brute force, O(rows times cols) for the DFS/BFS approach.
Most Important Observation: a fresh search should only start from a genuinely unvisited land cell.
Interview Difficulty: a very frequently asked, foundational medium-level grid DFS/BFS problem.
One line memory trick: sink each island once, count the sinks.
